Messages.Author: Carl Pilhatsch
Messages.Body:
Johannes Walch wrote:

>>oh and i forgot, you should use the swiss format.
>
>
> my magic days have been gone too long. what exactly is swiss format ?

Swiss should level the playing field and at the same time find the best
players.
Round 1 seating is assigned randomly.
Round 2: players who have 1 GW are seated together, and players who have
no GW are seated together as much as possible.
Round 3: players who have 2 GW are seated together, players with 1 GW
and players with 0 GW.
Round 4: and so on, you get it. :)

What does it serve? It levels out the field. Players who have low skill
and got lucky in round one will meet better players in round 2. If they
really were just lucky and have less skill, they will most likely not
get another GW in round 2.
Vice versa the other way round. If you were unlucky and got no GW, you
will have a greater chance of a GW if you are a really good player.
(There is stil luck involved, but that way, you get to recover from bad
luck a little bit).

Players are less likely to win 3 rounds in a row, as opposition gets
stronger in each round (theoretically).

That way, it would be a lot more likely to go to a final with less than
3 GW, and it would still be possible to get a good result (even if not
enough for the final) even if you lost all rounds and are starting the
last one.

This removes in part the "joker"-effect some players add to a game when
they have absolutely no chances to reach the final and act as
king-makers. With Swiss, things would be a bit more open until the end.

I'm also of the opinion that a continental Championship needs to have
more than 3 rounds, and I think that a true Champion needs to be good in
both limited and constructed format.
My proposal would be to have 3 rounds of limited (sealed or draft) on
day 1 and 3 rounds of constructed plus the final on day 2.
All 6 rounds would count together for determining who is going to the
final. That way things are still open after day 1 and players would show
up again on day 2.

To make things *still* more intersting, I'd propose the following: the
top *4* players are qualified for the final round. Players 5 to 9 will
have the opportunity to fight it out in one semi-final round before the
actual final round. Onle GW counts, no other tiebreakers - the player
with the GW goes as 5th into the final round. If no GW is achieved,
player *10* from the ranking goes to the final instead! :) This would
make it more interesting to achieve 10th rank. And it is an additional
incentive for the semi-finalists to play for a GW or lose everything.
The Semi-final round could have a shorter Time-limit (1hour) or players
start with 20 pool or players lose a pool at the start of each of their
turns as special rule to make things faster.

Next, I'd propose to have the ranking system a bit revised.
First GWs counts
Then VPs won with a GW
Then VPs not won with GW
Then TPs.

Makes VPs even more important, and makes players less inclined to give
VPs away in table-split deals.

So to summarize:

1. 3 rounds of limited *and* 3 rounds of constructed
2. Swiss system used
3. "semi-final" for ranked players 5-9 for last seat in final round
4. player ranked 10th gets last final round seat if no GW in semi-final
5. improve importance of VPs won in games where the player achieved a GW

Now that was a long post! :)

I hope some things will see use in the next series of continentals, or
at least at the EC.
Gogo for 200+ players in Germany next year! :)

Carl

Geography does certainly matter, a lot. Let's take for example someone
who resides in Paris. Discounting the Barcelona qualifier (since
they'd have to go there anyway, for the EC), within that same roughly
550-mile zone where a comparable player in Nebraska gets one qualifier
available, a Parisian has the following qualifiers: Paris, Germany,
Antwerp, Watford, Linz, and Kosice. (with several others only a little
further).

(why 550 miles? That's roughly a day's solid driving, and it's also
how far someone in the worst-case US scenario has to go to get to more
than one tourney.)

Yeah, it's 'not fair' that a player in a huge tournament like many of
the European ones has very little chance of qualifying percentage-wise
compared to say someone who plays in a 20-person tournament. But it's
also 'not fair' that someone with a modest travel budget can easily
attend a half-dozen qualifiers because they happen to live in a
geographically advantageous region than someone who lives in a more
remote area.

Note: I'm not picking on the Europeans here. Certain parts of the US
are equally condusive to this; a player in say Pittsburgh is in that
same range of the NAC qualifiers at Origins as well as the East
Central, Great Lakes, Toronto, Montreal, and Southeast ones, and the
Northeast isn't much farther. And it's 'not fair' that someone who
lives in Pittsburgh can get to six qualifiers with the ease that
someone in another part of the country can get to one or two.

Yes, it'd be nice to give a cookie to someone who does well in a 150+
person qualifier as opposed to a 20-person one. But many of the people
who play in smaller qualifiers simply can't *get* to the same number
of qualifiers as other players.

Shouldn't a person who finishes in the top 25% of the only tourney
they can attend be better rewarded than someone who goes to 6
qualifiers and places in the bottom half 5 times?

I'm highly, highly, highly opposed to the idea of Swiss format being
used for a continental championship. It's a terrible idea, for reasons
that are being discussed in the thread about Swiss format.

Short version: 'Swiss format' is designed as an optimizer for large
tournaments of games where matches are one-on-one, with no fair way to
distinguish between the quality-of-victory in two separate games.
V:tes is neither of these, and a Swiss format V:tes tournament can
result in a tangible advantage to a player (or several players) that
does worse in a given round than competing players.

-John Flournoy
